tagline: Master the Scrum framework and the ScrumMaster role from the Scrum Guide.

domains.name: Scrum Theory and Empiricism
domains.description: The empirical foundation of Scrum: transparency, inspection, adaptation, the Scrum values, and agile principles.

domains.name: Scrum Team Roles and Accountabilities
domains.description: Responsibilities and accountabilities of the Scrum Team, ScrumMaster, Product Owner, and Developers.

domains.name: Scrum Events
domains.description: The Sprint and its events: Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review, and Sprint Retrospective.

domains.name: Scrum Artifacts and Definition of Done
domains.description: The Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog, Increment, their commitments, and the Definition of Done.

domains.name: ScrumMaster Core Competencies
domains.description: Facilitation, coaching, teaching, and mentoring techniques the ScrumMaster uses to serve the team.

domains.name: Service to the Team, Product Owner, and Organization
domains.description: How the ScrumMaster supports the Product Owner and drives organizational change and impediment removal.

questions.stem: Scrum is founded on empiricism. Which three pillars uphold every empirical process?

options.text: Transparency, inspection, and adaptation
Commitment, focus, and courage
Planning, execution, and delivery
Estimation, prioritization, and reporting

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The Scrum Guide names transparency, inspection, and adaptation as the three pillars of the empirical process that underpins Scrum. Why the others are wrong: **B** commitment, focus, and courage are three of the five Scrum values, not the empirical pillars; **C** plan-execute-deliver describes a predictive lifecycle, not empiricism; **D** these are activities, not the foundational pillars of empirical process control.

questions.stem: A team holds events on schedule, but stakeholders frequently discover that the reported progress does not reflect the real state of the work. According to Scrum, which pillar is most directly being undermined?

options.text: Predictability
Velocity
Transparency
Standardization

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Inspection and adaptation are only useful when the artifacts and progress are transparent; when reported progress hides the real state, transparency is compromised and decisions are based on flawed information. Why the others are wrong: **A** predictability is an outcome of empiricism, not a pillar; **B** velocity is not a pillar of empiricism in the Scrum Guide; **D** standardization is not a Scrum pillar at all.

questions.stem: How many values does Scrum define, and what are they?

options.text: Four: individuals, working software, collaboration, and responding to change
Five: commitment, focus, openness, respect, and courage
Three: transparency, inspection, and adaptation
Seven: including simplicity and predictability

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The Scrum Guide defines five Scrum values: commitment, focus, openness, respect, and courage. Why the others are wrong: **A** these four are the Agile Manifesto values, not the Scrum values; **C** transparency, inspection, and adaptation are the three empirical pillars, not the values; **D** Scrum defines exactly five values, and simplicity/predictability are not among them.

questions.stem: Is Scrum best described as a methodology or a framework, and why does the distinction matter?

options.text: A maturity model: it ranks teams by capability level as they adopt more practices
A methodology: it prescribes a complete, detailed set of techniques and tools that teams must follow exactly
A process: it defines a fixed sequence of steps that produces the same output every time
A framework: it is purposely incomplete, defining only the parts required to implement Scrum theory, and teams add the practices that fit their context

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** The Scrum Guide describes Scrum as a lightweight framework that is purposefully incomplete, defining only the parts required to implement Scrum theory, so teams add complementary practices that suit them. Why the others are wrong: **A** Scrum is not a maturity model and does not rank teams by level; **B** a methodology prescribes detailed techniques, which Scrum deliberately does not; **C** Scrum is not a deterministic fixed-step process.

questions.stem: Which statement best reflects a core value of the Agile Manifesto?

options.text: We value responding to change over following a plan
We value comprehensive documentation over working software
We value contract negotiation over customer collaboration
We value processes and tools over individuals and interactions

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The Agile Manifesto values responding to change over following a plan, while still acknowledging value in the item on the right. Why the others are wrong: **B** the Manifesto values working software over comprehensive documentation, so this reverses it; **C** it values customer collaboration over contract negotiation, the opposite of this; **D** it values individuals and interactions over processes and tools, again reversed.

questions.stem: A ScrumMaster wants to apply lean thinking to the team's process. Which focus is most consistent with lean thinking as referenced by Scrum?

options.text: Maximizing resource utilization so no one is ever idle
Reducing waste and focusing on the essentials that add value
Increasing documentation so every decision is fully recorded
Adding extra approval gates to catch defects before delivery

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Lean thinking, which Scrum draws on, centers on reducing waste and focusing on the essentials, complementing Scrum's empirical, lightweight design. Why the others are wrong: **A** maximizing utilization often creates queues and waste, which is contrary to lean; **C** more documentation for its own sake is non-value-adding work; **D** extra approval gates add handoffs and delay, classic forms of waste.

questions.stem: Why does Scrum prescribe regular, time-boxed events rather than letting the team inspect and adapt whenever it feels necessary?

options.text: The events replace the need for any informal collaboration during the Sprint
The events exist mainly to give management fixed checkpoints to approve the team's work
The events create formal, cadenced opportunities to inspect and adapt, reducing the need for other meetings and increasing transparency
The events are optional rituals that mature teams eventually outgrow

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Each Scrum event is a formal opportunity to inspect and adapt Scrum artifacts; holding them on a regular cadence creates transparency and reduces the need for meetings not defined in Scrum. Why the others are wrong: **A** events complement, not replace, ongoing collaboration; **B** the events serve the Scrum Team's empirical control, not management approval; **D** the events are required and are not outgrown.

questions.stem: The Scrum Guide 2020 refers to the three roles on a Scrum Team using a specific term. Which term and set is correct?

options.text: Four roles: Scrum Master, Product Owner, Developers, and Stakeholders
Three roles: Scrum Master, Product Owner, and Project Manager
Three accountabilities: Scrum Master, Business Analyst, and Developers
Three accountabilities: Scrum Master, Product Owner, and Developers

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** The Scrum Guide 2020 speaks of three accountabilities within one Scrum Team: the Scrum Master, the Product Owner, and the Developers. Why the others are wrong: **A** stakeholders are not part of the Scrum Team, and there are three accountabilities, not four; **B** Scrum has no Project Manager accountability; **C** Business Analyst is not a Scrum accountability and replaces the Product Owner here.

questions.stem: Who is accountable for managing the Product Backlog, including ordering its items and ensuring it is transparent and understood?

options.text: The Product Owner
The Scrum Master
The Developers collectively
The most senior stakeholder

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The Product Owner is accountable for effective Product Backlog management, including developing the Product Goal, ordering items, and making the backlog transparent and understood. Why the others are wrong: **B** the Scrum Master serves the Product Owner but does not own the backlog; **C** the Developers may help refine items but are not accountable for ordering the backlog; **D** stakeholders provide input but hold no accountability for the backlog.

questions.stem: A development manager insists the Product Owner role be filled by a three-person committee so decisions are shared. Why does Scrum specify that the Product Owner is one person?

options.text: Scrum allows multiple Product Owners per team to spread the workload
A committee is acceptable as long as members vote on every backlog item
The Product Owner is one person so the backlog has a single, clear voice; a committee can represent stakeholders' needs through that one person
The Scrum Master can break ties when the committee disagrees

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** The Scrum Guide states the Product Owner is one person, not a committee; those wanting to change the backlog can do so by trying to convince that single Product Owner, keeping accountability and the ordering clear. Why the others are wrong: **A** Scrum does not define multiple Product Owners for one team; **B** a voting committee dilutes the single accountability Scrum requires; **D** the Scrum Master does not arbitrate backlog decisions.

questions.stem: During a Sprint, a stakeholder approaches a Developer directly and tries to reorder the Product Backlog to insert a pet feature. According to Scrum, what is the correct understanding of backlog authority?

options.text: Any stakeholder may reorder the Product Backlog if a Developer agrees
Only the Product Owner's decision on Product Backlog order is authoritative; for it to change, others must influence the Product Owner
The Developers own the order of the Product Backlog during the Sprint
The Scrum Master approves all changes to the Product Backlog order

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The Product Owner has sole authority over the order of the Product Backlog; for the order to change, people must convince the Product Owner. Why the others are wrong: **A** a stakeholder cannot reorder the backlog by persuading a single Developer; **C** Developers own the Sprint Backlog, not the order of the Product Backlog; **D** the Scrum Master facilitates but does not approve backlog ordering.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the Developers' accountability on a Scrum Team?

options.text: They are accountable for approving the release of each Increment to customers
They are accountable for ordering the Product Backlog by business value
They are accountable for removing organizational impediments outside the team
They are accountable for creating a usable Increment each Sprint and for the quality through adherence to a Definition of Done

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** The Developers are accountable for creating a plan for the Sprint, instilling quality by adhering to a Definition of Done, and producing a usable Increment each Sprint. Why the others are wrong: **A** the Product Owner, not the Developers, decides on releasing the Increment; **B** ordering the Product Backlog is the Product Owner's accountability; **C** addressing organizational impediments is primarily the Scrum Master's service to the organization.

questions.stem: Which two of the following are accountabilities of the Scrum Master as defined by the Scrum Guide? (Select two.)

options.text: Coaching the team members in self-management and cross-functionality
Helping the Scrum Team and organization understand and enact Scrum
Deciding the order of items in the Product Backlog
Writing all of the team's user stories and acceptance criteria

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** The Scrum Master is a true leader who coaches the team in self-management and cross-functionality, and helps everyone understand Scrum theory and practice both within the team and across the organization. Why the others are wrong: **C** ordering the Product Backlog is the Product Owner's accountability, not the Scrum Master's; **D** authoring stories and criteria is work for the Product Owner and Developers, not a Scrum Master accountability.

questions.stem: A Scrum Team of eleven Developers struggles to coordinate and stay cohesive. What guidance does the Scrum Guide give about Scrum Team size?

options.text: There is no recommended size; teams of any size work equally well
The Scrum Team is typically 10 or fewer people; if it is too large, it should consider reorganizing into multiple cohesive Scrum Teams on the same product
A Scrum Team must always have exactly seven Developers plus two
Large teams should add a second Scrum Master to manage the extra Developers

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The Scrum Guide says the Scrum Team is small, typically 10 or fewer people; if teams become too large, they should consider reorganizing into multiple cohesive Scrum Teams focused on the same product with a shared Product Goal. Why the others are wrong: **A** size does matter for communication and cohesion; **C** the old 7±2 Development Team guidance was removed in 2020; **D** Scrum has one Scrum Master per team, and adding one does not fix size.

questions.stem: Which phrase best describes the leadership style the Scrum Guide associates with the Scrum Master?

options.text: An administrator whose main job is scheduling meetings and taking notes
A command-and-control manager who assigns tasks to Developers
A true leader who serves the Scrum Team and the larger organization
A gatekeeper who approves the team's work before it ships

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** The Scrum Guide describes the Scrum Master as a true leader who serves the Scrum Team and the larger organization. Why the others are wrong: **A** reducing the role to administration ignores its coaching and leadership accountabilities; **B** command-and-control task assignment contradicts the self-managing nature of the team; **D** the Scrum Master is not an approval gate for the team's work.

questions.stem: Which Scrum event is described as the container for all other events?

options.text: The Sprint
Sprint Planning
The Daily Scrum
The Sprint Review

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The Sprint is a fixed-length event of one month or less and is the container for all other Scrum events: Sprint Planning, Daily Scrums, the Sprint Review, and the Sprint Retrospective. Why the others are wrong: **B** Sprint Planning happens inside the Sprint, so it cannot contain it; **C** the Daily Scrum occurs within the Sprint; **D** the Sprint Review is one of the events held inside the Sprint.

questions.stem: What is the maximum time-box for Sprint Planning for a one-month Sprint?

options.text: There is no time-box for Sprint Planning
Two hours
Four hours
Eight hours

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Sprint Planning is time-boxed to a maximum of eight hours for a one-month Sprint and is usually shorter for shorter Sprints. Why the others are wrong: **A** Sprint Planning does have a time-box in Scrum; **B** two hours is far below the maximum for a one-month Sprint; **C** four hours is also below the eight-hour maximum for a one-month Sprint.

questions.stem: During the Daily Scrum, the Scrum Master notices it has become a status meeting where Developers report progress to her. What is the intended purpose of the Daily Scrum?

options.text: For Developers to give a daily status report to the Scrum Master
For the Developers to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the Sprint Backlog, planning their work for the next day
For the Product Owner to reassign tasks and reprioritize the Sprint Backlog
For stakeholders to review completed work and provide feedback

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The Daily Scrum is for the Developers to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the Sprint Backlog as needed, planning their next day of work. Why the others are wrong: **A** it is not a status report to the Scrum Master, who need not even run it; **C** the Product Owner does not reassign tasks at the Daily Scrum; **D** stakeholder feedback belongs to the Sprint Review, not the Daily Scrum.

questions.stem: What is the time-box for the Daily Scrum?

options.text: It varies with Sprint length
30 minutes
60 minutes
15 minutes

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event for the Developers, held at the same time and place each working day of the Sprint. Why the others are wrong: **A** unlike most events, the Daily Scrum is a fixed 15 minutes regardless of Sprint length; **B** 30 minutes exceeds the 15-minute time-box; **C** 60 minutes is far beyond the time-box.

questions.stem: The purpose of the Sprint Review is best described as which of the following?

options.text: To inspect the outcome of the Sprint with stakeholders and determine future adaptations, including to the Product Backlog
For the team to privately reflect on how to improve its process and interactions
For the Scrum Master to formally sign off that the Sprint is complete
For the Developers to plan the work of the upcoming Sprint

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The Sprint Review is a working session where the Scrum Team and stakeholders inspect the Increment and the Sprint's outcome and collaborate on what to do next, often adjusting the Product Backlog. Why the others are wrong: **B** private process reflection is the Sprint Retrospective; **C** the Scrum Master does not sign off on Sprints; **D** planning the next Sprint's work is Sprint Planning.

questions.stem: Under pressure to deliver more features, a manager proposes that the team skip the Sprint Retrospective for several Sprints. What is the most likely consequence according to Scrum's intent?

options.text: Nothing changes, because the Retrospective is an optional event in Scrum
The team will deliver more value because it spends all its time building
The team loses its dedicated opportunity to inspect itself and plan improvements, weakening continuous improvement and adaptation
The Sprint Review will automatically cover the same improvement discussions

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** The Sprint Retrospective is the team's dedicated opportunity to inspect how the last Sprint went regarding people, relationships, process, and tools, and to plan improvements; skipping it removes a key inspect-and-adapt loop. Why the others are wrong: **A** the Retrospective is a required Scrum event, not optional; **B** dropping improvement work tends to erode effectiveness over time; **D** the Review focuses on the product, not the team's own process.

questions.stem: Halfway through a Sprint, a major market shift makes the Sprint Goal obsolete. Who can cancel the Sprint, and on what basis?

options.text: A Sprint can never be canceled once it has started
Any Developer may cancel the Sprint if the work becomes too difficult
The Scrum Master cancels the Sprint when the team falls behind schedule
Only the Product Owner has the authority to cancel a Sprint, and may do so if the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** The Scrum Guide states that a Sprint could be cancelled if the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete, and only the Product Owner has the authority to cancel the Sprint. Why the others are wrong: **A** Sprints can be cancelled, though it is rare; **B** Developers cannot unilaterally cancel a Sprint, and difficulty alone is not the criterion; **C** the Scrum Master does not hold cancellation authority.

questions.stem: During Sprint Planning, which two topics must the Scrum Team address? (Select two.)

options.text: Why is this Sprint valuable, which leads to crafting the Sprint Goal
What can be Done this Sprint, selecting Product Backlog items for the Sprint
Which individual will be assigned each task by the Scrum Master
How the team performed on velocity in every prior Sprint of the year

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Sprint Planning addresses why the Sprint is valuable (the Sprint Goal), what can be done (selecting items), and how the work will be accomplished; the first two are core topics here. Why the others are wrong: **C** the Scrum Master does not assign tasks to individuals; the Developers self-manage their work; **D** a full historical velocity review is not a required Sprint Planning topic.

questions.stem: Place these Scrum events in the order they typically occur within a single Sprint, from the start of the Sprint to its end.

options.text: Sprint Planning
Daily Scrum (held each day of the Sprint)
Sprint Review
Sprint Retrospective

questions.explanation: A Sprint begins with Sprint Planning, where the team crafts the Sprint Goal and plans the work. Throughout the Sprint, the Developers hold a Daily Scrum each working day to inspect progress and adapt their plan. Near the end of the Sprint, the Sprint Review inspects the Increment with stakeholders, and finally the Sprint Retrospective closes the Sprint by inspecting how the team worked and planning improvements before the next Sprint begins.

questions.stem: A Scrum Team raises an impediment that it can resolve internally, such as agreeing on a shared coding standard. How should the Scrum Master help the team address impediments like this?

options.text: Personally fix every impediment the team encounters, large or small, so the team can keep coding
Coach the team to resolve impediments within its control itself, stepping in only for those it cannot remove on its own
Tell the team that impediment removal is solely management's responsibility
Record the impediment but take no action until the next Sprint Retrospective

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The Scrum Master helps the team address and remove impediments, which means coaching the self-managing team to resolve what is within its control and stepping in to clear or escalate only those it cannot remove alone. Why the others are wrong: **A** fixing every small impediment fosters dependence and undercuts self-management; **C** impediment removal is not solely management's job; **D** delaying action on a removable impediment needlessly blocks the team.

questions.stem: Each Scrum artifact contains a commitment. Which commitment belongs to the Product Backlog?

options.text: The Product Goal
The Sprint Goal
The Definition of Done
The release plan

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** In the Scrum Guide 2020, the Product Backlog's commitment is the Product Goal, which describes a future state of the product the team plans toward. Why the others are wrong: **B** the Sprint Goal is the commitment for the Sprint Backlog; **C** the Definition of Done is the commitment for the Increment; **D** a release plan is not a Scrum artifact commitment.

questions.stem: Which commitment is associated with the Sprint Backlog?

options.text: The Definition of Done
The Product Goal
The Sprint Goal
The Sprint burndown chart

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** The Sprint Backlog's commitment is the Sprint Goal, the single objective for the Sprint that gives the Developers focus and coherence. Why the others are wrong: **A** the Definition of Done is the Increment's commitment; **B** the Product Goal is the Product Backlog's commitment; **D** a burndown chart is an optional tool, not the Sprint Backlog's commitment.

questions.stem: A Product Owner asks what the Definition of Done formally describes. Which answer is correct per Scrum?

options.text: A ranking of Product Backlog items by business value
A list of all Product Backlog items planned for the next release
The objective the team commits to achieving during the Sprint
A formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** The Definition of Done is a formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product; work is not part of an Increment until it meets the DoD. Why the others are wrong: **A** value-ranking is Product Backlog ordering, done by the Product Owner; **B** a release item list is not the DoD; **C** that describes the Sprint Goal.

questions.stem: An organization has a standard set of quality criteria all products must meet. According to Scrum, how should a Scrum Team set its Definition of Done in this case?

options.text: The team ignores organizational standards and invents an unrelated Definition of Done
If organizational standards exist, the Scrum Team must follow them as a minimum and may add stricter criteria of its own
Only the Scrum Master may write the Definition of Done
The Definition of Done is set once at company founding and never changes

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** When organizational standards for a Definition of Done exist, all Scrum Teams must follow them as a minimum; if none exist, the Scrum Team creates one appropriate for the product, and teams may make it stricter. Why the others are wrong: **A** ignoring mandatory standards violates Scrum's guidance; **C** the whole Scrum Team, not just the Scrum Master, shapes the DoD; **D** the DoD can evolve as the team and product mature.

questions.stem: A team repeatedly marks items 'done' that later require rework because tests and documentation were skipped. Which approach best reflects the advantages of a strong Definition of Done?

options.text: Remove the Definition of Done entirely so the team moves faster
Loosen the Definition of Done so more items can be reported as complete each Sprint
Strengthen the Definition of Done so 'done' means truly releasable, increasing transparency and reducing accumulated technical debt
Keep the same Definition of Done but stop demonstrating the Increment at the Sprint Review

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A strong Definition of Done makes the true state of work transparent and ensures each Increment is genuinely usable, which curbs the technical debt that causes rework. Why the others are wrong: **A** removing it destroys transparency about quality; **B** loosening the DoD hides incomplete work and worsens rework; **D** hiding the Increment reduces inspection and does nothing to address the quality gap.

questions.stem: Which two statements about the Increment are correct according to the Scrum Guide? (Select two.)

options.text: An Increment is a concrete stepping stone toward the Product Goal and must be usable
Multiple Increments may be created within a single Sprint
Work can be considered part of an Increment even if it does not meet the Definition of Done
An Increment may only be delivered at the very end of the Sprint, never during it

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Each Increment is a usable stepping stone toward the Product Goal, and the Scrum Guide notes that multiple Increments may be created within a Sprint. Why the others are wrong: **C** work that does not meet the Definition of Done is not an Increment and cannot be presented as done; **D** an Increment may be delivered to stakeholders before the end of the Sprint, not only at the Sprint Review.

questions.stem: Who is responsible for the Sprint Backlog, and what does it represent?

options.text: Stakeholders own the Sprint Backlog and set its scope at the Sprint Review
The Product Owner owns the Sprint Backlog and assigns its tasks each day
The Scrum Master owns the Sprint Backlog and tracks each Developer's hours
The Developers own the Sprint Backlog; it is their plan, by and for them, to deliver the Increment and meet the Sprint Goal

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** The Sprint Backlog is composed of the Sprint Goal, the selected Product Backlog items, and the plan for delivering the Increment; it is a plan by and for the Developers, who own it. Why the others are wrong: **A** stakeholders do not own or scope the Sprint Backlog; **B** the Product Owner owns the Product Backlog, not the Sprint Backlog; **C** the Scrum Master does not own or hour-track the Sprint Backlog.

questions.stem: A Scrum Master is deciding whether to facilitate, teach, mentor, or coach in a given moment. Which description correctly distinguishes coaching?

options.text: Coaching uses questions to help people find their own answers and grow their capability, rather than supplying the answer directly
Coaching means giving the team the correct technical solution so they can implement it quickly
Coaching means making decisions on the team's behalf to keep things moving
Coaching means documenting the team's process so others can follow it

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Coaching is a non-directive stance that uses powerful questions to help people discover their own solutions and build lasting capability, distinct from teaching or simply giving answers. Why the others are wrong: **B** supplying the technical solution is closer to teaching or consulting, not coaching; **C** deciding for the team undermines self-management; **D** documenting process is neither coaching nor a defining feature of it.

questions.stem: When is facilitation by the Scrum Master most appropriate?

options.text: When the Scrum Master wants to dictate the final decision to save time
When a group needs help having a productive, inclusive conversation and reaching a decision without the facilitator imposing the outcome
Only during the Sprint Review and never during other events
When the team must be prevented from participating in the decision

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Facilitation helps a group hold a productive, inclusive discussion and converge on a decision while the facilitator stays neutral on the content. Why the others are wrong: **A** dictating the outcome is the opposite of facilitating; **C** facilitation is useful across many situations, not just the Sprint Review; **D** good facilitation increases participation rather than blocking it.

questions.stem: A Scrum Master wants the team to reach a decision that everyone can support, even if it is not everyone's first choice. Which group decision-making technique best fits this goal?

options.text: Avoiding any decision until the team naturally forgets the issue
Letting the loudest person decide so the discussion ends quickly
Having the Scrum Master cast the deciding vote on all matters
Seeking consent (no one has a strong objection) rather than requiring unanimous consensus

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Consent-based decision making asks whether anyone has a serious objection, producing a decision the group can support without demanding unanimous enthusiasm, which is often faster and more durable than strict consensus. Why the others are wrong: **A** avoiding the decision resolves nothing; **B** deferring to the loudest voice ignores the group and harms safety; **C** the Scrum Master deciding for the team undermines self-management.

questions.stem: A Developer is blocked because a build server keeps failing, and the team cannot fix it alone. What is the most appropriate first action for the Scrum Master?

options.text: Reassign the blocked Developer to a different team permanently
Tell the Developer to work around it quietly and not mention it again
Help the team make the impediment visible and work to resolve or escalate it so the team's flow is restored
Cancel the Sprint because of the blocker

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** The Scrum Master causes the removal of impediments to the Scrum Team's progress, which includes making the impediment transparent and resolving or escalating it appropriately. Why the others are wrong: **A** permanently reassigning a Developer is a disruptive overreaction, not impediment removal; **B** hiding the impediment reduces transparency and leaves the team blocked; **D** only the Product Owner can cancel a Sprint, and a build issue is not grounds for it.

questions.stem: Which development practice most directly helps a Scrum Team reduce technical debt and protect a strong Definition of Done?

options.text: Skipping code review to deliver features faster
Deferring all testing to a separate phase after several Sprints
Avoiding refactoring so the codebase is never disturbed
Continuous integration with automated testing so defects are caught early and often

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Continuous integration with automated tests gives rapid feedback and keeps the Increment close to releasable, which directly limits technical debt and supports a robust Definition of Done. Why the others are wrong: **A** skipping review removes a key quality check and increases debt; **B** deferring testing lets defects and debt pile up; **C** avoiding refactoring allows debt to accumulate as the design decays.

questions.stem: Which two behaviors are consistent with the Scrum Master acting as a true leader for the Scrum Team? (Select two.)

options.text: Fostering an environment of psychological safety where the team can self-manage
Removing impediments that are beyond the team's ability to resolve
Assigning each task to a specific Developer and tracking their hours
Approving the team's technical decisions before any work can begin

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** A true leader creates a safe, self-managing environment and clears impediments the team cannot remove on its own, serving rather than directing. Why the others are wrong: **C** assigning tasks and tracking hours is command-and-control that undercuts self-management; **D** gating the team's technical decisions removes their autonomy and contradicts servant leadership.

questions.stem: How does teaching differ from mentoring in the Scrum Master's stance toolkit?

options.text: Teaching and mentoring are identical and interchangeable terms
Teaching imparts specific knowledge or skills, while mentoring shares experience and guidance over time based on a relationship
Teaching means deciding for the team, while mentoring means ignoring the team
Teaching is only done by managers, and mentoring only by executives

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Teaching transfers concrete knowledge or skills (for example, how Scrum works), whereas mentoring draws on the mentor's experience to guide someone's growth through an ongoing relationship. Why the others are wrong: **A** they are distinct stances, not interchangeable; **C** neither stance is about deciding for or ignoring the team; **D** these stances are not restricted by job title.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a way the Scrum Master serves the Product Owner?

options.text: Helping find techniques for effective Product Goal definition and Product Backlog management
Taking over ordering the Product Backlog so the Product Owner can focus elsewhere
Deciding which stakeholders the Product Owner is allowed to talk to
Writing the Product Owner's performance review for management

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The Scrum Master serves the Product Owner by helping find techniques for effective Product Goal definition and Product Backlog management, among other supports. Why the others are wrong: **B** the Scrum Master does not take over backlog ordering, which is the Product Owner's accountability; **C** controlling stakeholder access is not a Scrum Master service; **D** writing performance reviews is not part of the Scrum Master's service to the Product Owner.

questions.stem: A traditional organization adopting Scrum keeps asking, 'Who is the project manager on this Scrum Team?' What is the most accurate response?

options.text: The Product Owner is the project manager because they control the budget
The Scrum Master is simply the new title for the project manager
Scrum does not define a project manager; its accountabilities are distributed across the Product Owner, the Scrum Master, and the Developers
Every Scrum Team must appoint a project manager in addition to the three accountabilities

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Scrum has no project manager; the work traditionally assigned to that role is spread across the three accountabilities, with the Product Owner handling value and the backlog, the Developers self-managing the work, and the Scrum Master enabling effectiveness. Why the others are wrong: **A** the Product Owner is accountable for value, not classic project management; **B** the Scrum Master is a servant leader, not a rebranded project manager; **D** Scrum defines exactly three accountabilities and adds no project manager.

questions.stem: A recurring delay is caused by a separate department that must approve every deployment, sitting outside the Scrum Team. How should the Scrum Master treat this?

options.text: As acceptable overhead the team should simply absorb every Sprint
As an organizational impediment to be made visible and addressed by working with the wider organization to remove or reduce it
As a reason to lower the Definition of Done so approvals are unnecessary
As a problem only the Developers should solve without involving the organization

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Part of the Scrum Master's service to the organization is identifying and helping remove impediments that lie beyond the team, such as cross-departmental bottlenecks, by working with the wider organization. Why the others are wrong: **A** absorbing systemic waste indefinitely ignores the Scrum Master's accountability to improve it; **C** weakening the Definition of Done sacrifices quality to dodge the problem; **D** organizational impediments require organizational engagement, not the Developers alone.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes how adopting Scrum can affect organizational design?

options.text: It has no effect on organizational structure because Scrum is only a team practice
It requires adding more layers of management to oversee each Scrum Team
It mandates that all departments be merged into a single team
It can drive changes toward cross-functional, self-managing teams and away from rigid functional silos and handoffs

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Adopting Scrum often pushes the organization toward cross-functional, self-managing teams and fewer silos and handoffs, since those structures best support empirical delivery of value. Why the others are wrong: **A** Scrum's effects routinely extend beyond a single team into organizational design; **B** adding management layers contradicts self-management; **C** Scrum does not require merging all departments into one team.

questions.stem: A new Product Owner struggles to keep the Product Backlog ordered and understood by stakeholders. Which support from the Scrum Master is most appropriate?

options.text: Tell the Product Owner that backlog management is not the Scrum Master's concern
Quietly reorder the backlog for the Product Owner each Sprint
Coach the Product Owner on Product Backlog management techniques and help facilitate stakeholder collaboration
Ask the Developers to take over all Product Owner decisions

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** The Scrum Master supports an effective Product Backlog management approach by coaching the Product Owner on techniques and facilitating collaboration with stakeholders, building the Product Owner's capability. Why the others are wrong: **A** supporting the Product Owner is squarely part of the Scrum Master's service; **B** secretly reordering the backlog usurps the Product Owner's accountability; **D** shifting Product Owner decisions to Developers violates the accountabilities.

questions.stem: Which two are genuine ways the Scrum Master serves the wider organization? (Select two.)

options.text: Leading and coaching the organization in its Scrum adoption
Helping employees and stakeholders understand and enact an empirical approach to complex work
Setting individual sales targets for each department
Approving the company's annual financial budget

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** The Scrum Master serves the organization by leading and coaching its Scrum adoption and by helping employees and stakeholders understand and enact an empirical approach to complex work. Why the others are wrong: **C** setting departmental sales targets is a management function outside the Scrum Master's defined service; **D** approving financial budgets is not a Scrum Master accountability.

questions.stem: A team has high transparency and inspects its work often, but never changes anything based on what it learns. Which pillar of empiricism is effectively broken?

options.text: Transparency, because the work is no longer visible
Inspection, because the team has stopped looking at its work
Commitment, because the team is not focused
Adaptation, because inspection is not leading to any adjustment

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** The Scrum Guide warns that inspection without adaptation is pointless; if a team learns something but never adjusts, the adaptation pillar fails even when transparency and inspection are healthy. Why the others are wrong: **A** the scenario states transparency is high, so it is not broken; **B** inspection is described as frequent here, so it is intact; **C** commitment is a Scrum value, not a pillar of empiricism.

questions.stem: A Developer admits in front of the team that a feature she built last Sprint has a serious flaw, even though saying so is uncomfortable. Which Scrum value is she most directly demonstrating?

options.text: Focus
Courage
Commitment
Respect

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Courage is the Scrum value of being brave enough to do the right thing and work on tough problems, including admitting difficult truths. Why the others are wrong: **A** focus concerns concentrating on the Sprint's work, not speaking up about a flaw; **C** commitment is about dedication to goals, not candor under discomfort; **D** respect is about valuing others as capable people, which is not the central act here.

questions.stem: Which statement best reflects the Agile Manifesto principle about delivering software?

options.text: Deliver a single large release at the very end of the project to minimize disruption
Deliver working software frequently, from a couple of weeks to a couple of months, preferring the shorter timescale
Deliver only once all requirements have been fully documented and signed off
Deliver software only after a separate quality assurance phase completes

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** An Agile Manifesto principle states that teams deliver working software frequently, from a couple of weeks to a couple of months, with a preference for the shorter timescale. Why the others are wrong: **A** a single end-of-project release contradicts frequent delivery; **C** waiting for fully signed-off requirements is a predictive, document-heavy approach; **D** gating delivery behind a separate QA phase delays the frequent flow of working software.

questions.stem: An executive asks why Scrum keeps Sprints short rather than running one long cycle to a fixed plan. Which explanation best reflects empirical process control?

options.text: Short Sprints guarantee that the original plan will be delivered exactly as written
Short Sprints limit risk to one short period of cost and effort and create frequent points to inspect reality and adapt the plan
Short Sprints exist mainly so management can hold the team to tighter deadlines
Short Sprints remove the need to plan because the work is so small

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Empiricism manages risk through frequent inspection and adaptation; shorter Sprints cap the risk and cost exposed at any time and give the team regular opportunities to adjust to what is actually learned. Why the others are wrong: **A** empiricism expects the plan to change, not be delivered unchanged; **C** Sprints serve the team's empirical control, not tighter management deadlines; **D** Sprints still require planning, such as Sprint Planning.

questions.stem: Which two ideas are central to lean thinking as it informs Scrum? (Select two.)

options.text: Reducing waste so effort concentrates on what adds value
Focusing on the essentials and removing non-value-adding work
Maximizing work in progress to keep everyone fully loaded
Adding inspection gates and handoffs to control every step

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Lean thinking, which Scrum draws on, reduces waste and focuses on the essentials so that effort is spent on value rather than overhead. Why the others are wrong: **C** maximizing work in progress creates queues and delay, a form of waste that lean opposes; **D** extra gates and handoffs add non-value-adding steps, the opposite of lean's intent.

questions.stem: A coach argues that two teams using identical tools and ceremonies should produce identical results, and is surprised when they do not. Which idea best explains why Scrum expects different outcomes?

options.text: Scrum is a defined process, so identical inputs must yield identical outputs
Scrum is a framework applied to complex, often unpredictable work, so each team adapts practices to its context and learns empirically
Scrum guarantees the same velocity for any two teams of the same size
Differences only occur when a team is doing Scrum incorrectly

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Scrum is a lightweight framework for complex work where cause and effect are not fully predictable, so teams inspect, adapt, and add context-specific practices, leading to different valid outcomes. Why the others are wrong: **A** Scrum is explicitly not a deterministic defined process for complex work; **C** Scrum makes no promise of equal velocity, which is not even comparable across teams; **D** divergent outcomes are normal in complex work, not proof of doing Scrum wrong.

questions.stem: A manager states that the Developers should be held accountable as individuals for any item that is not finished. What does the Scrum Guide say about accountability on the Scrum Team?

options.text: Each Developer is individually accountable to management for their assigned items
The Scrum Master is personally accountable for any unfinished work
While individuals have specialized skills, accountability belongs to the Scrum Team as a whole
Only the Product Owner is accountable for delivery outcomes

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** The Scrum Guide states that although individuals may have specialized skills and areas of focus, accountability belongs to the Scrum Team as a whole. Why the others are wrong: **A** Scrum does not assign individual delivery accountability to Developers for separate items; **B** the Scrum Master is not accountable for the team's unfinished work; **D** the Product Owner is accountable for value, not as the sole owner of delivery outcomes.

questions.stem: A new ScrumMaster asks what it means that the Scrum Team is 'cross-functional.' Which description is correct per the Scrum Guide?

options.text: Each member can perform every other member's job interchangeably
The team relies on outside departments for most of the skills it needs
The team members collectively have all the skills needed to create value each Sprint
The team rotates a different functional manager into the team each Sprint

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Cross-functional means the Scrum Team has, among its members, all the skills necessary to create value each Sprint without depending on others outside the team. Why the others are wrong: **A** cross-functional does not require every person to do every job; it is a team-level property; **B** depending on outside departments for core skills is the opposite of cross-functional; **D** Scrum does not rotate functional managers into the team.

questions.stem: Who within the Scrum Team is accountable for instilling quality by adhering to a Definition of Done?

options.text: The Developers
The Product Owner
The ScrumMaster
The quality assurance department

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Among the Developers' accountabilities, the Scrum Guide lists instilling quality by adhering to a Definition of Done. Why the others are wrong: **B** the Product Owner is accountable for value and the Product Backlog, not for instilling build quality; **C** the ScrumMaster fosters effectiveness but does not own adherence to the Definition of Done; **D** a separate QA department is not part of the Scrum Team's accountabilities in Scrum.

questions.stem: A Product Owner delegates the writing and ordering of some Product Backlog items to the Developers. According to Scrum, what remains true about accountability?

options.text: Delegation transfers backlog accountability to whoever does the work
Once delegated, the ScrumMaster becomes accountable for the backlog
Delegation is forbidden; only the Product Owner may ever touch the backlog
The Product Owner remains accountable for the Product Backlog even when others do the work

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** The Product Owner may have others manage the Product Backlog, but the Product Owner remains accountable for it. Why the others are wrong: **A** delegating the work does not transfer the accountability; **B** the ScrumMaster never becomes accountable for the Product Backlog; **C** delegation of backlog work is explicitly allowed in Scrum, with accountability staying put.

questions.stem: Two Developers ask the ScrumMaster to assign who works on which task each morning so things feel organized. What is the best ScrumMaster response, given the Developers' accountability?

options.text: Begin assigning tasks daily to each Developer to give them clarity
Ask the Product Owner to assign the tasks instead
Coach the Developers to self-manage and decide among themselves who does what, while helping them build that capability
Escalate to the functional manager to assign the work formally

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** The Developers are self-managing and decide who does what and how; the ScrumMaster coaches them to organize their own work rather than assigning it. Why the others are wrong: **A** assigning tasks undermines self-management, a core Developer accountability; **B** the Product Owner does not assign Developer tasks; **D** routing work assignment to a functional manager reintroduces command-and-control that Scrum avoids.

questions.stem: How does the Scrum Guide characterize the relationship between the three accountabilities and the Scrum Team structure?

options.text: There are separate sub-teams reporting up to a team lead
There are no sub-teams or hierarchies; it is one cohesive unit focused on one Product Goal at a time
The Developers are a sub-team managed by the ScrumMaster
The Product Owner sits above the team in a reporting hierarchy

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The Scrum Guide states the Scrum Team has no sub-teams or hierarchies; it is one cohesive unit of professionals focused on one Product Goal at a time. Why the others are wrong: **A** sub-teams reporting to a lead contradict the single cohesive unit; **C** the Developers are not a sub-team managed by the ScrumMaster; **D** the Product Owner is an accountability within the team, not a layer above it.

questions.stem: Which two activities are accountabilities of the Product Owner according to the Scrum Guide? (Select two.)

options.text: Developing and explicitly communicating the Product Goal
Ensuring the Product Backlog is transparent, visible, and understood
Facilitating the Sprint Retrospective for the team
Coaching the organization in its Scrum adoption

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** The Product Owner is accountable for developing and explicitly communicating the Product Goal and for ensuring the Product Backlog is transparent, visible, and understood. Why the others are wrong: **C** facilitating events and coaching the team is the ScrumMaster's domain, not a Product Owner accountability; **D** coaching the organization in Scrum adoption is part of the ScrumMaster's service to the organization.

questions.stem: A team wants to start a new Sprint a week after the previous one ends so people can 'catch up' on email. What does the Scrum Guide say about the timing between Sprints?

options.text: A gap of up to one week between Sprints is recommended for recovery
Teams should leave several days between Sprints to plan the next one
The interval between Sprints is set by management each quarter
A new Sprint starts immediately after the conclusion of the previous Sprint

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** The Scrum Guide states that a new Sprint starts immediately after the conclusion of the previous Sprint, keeping a continuous cadence. Why the others are wrong: **A** Scrum prescribes no recovery gap between Sprints; **B** planning the next Sprint happens in Sprint Planning inside the new Sprint, not in a gap; **C** the cadence is fixed by Scrum, not set per quarter by management.

questions.stem: What is the maximum length of a Sprint according to the Scrum Guide?

options.text: One week
Two weeks
One month
One quarter

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Sprints are fixed-length events of one month or less, so one month is the maximum Sprint length. Why the others are wrong: **A** one week is a valid Sprint length but not the maximum; **B** two weeks is common but not the upper limit; **D** a quarter far exceeds the one-month maximum and would reduce the chance to inspect and adapt.

questions.stem: During Sprint Planning, after deciding why the Sprint is valuable and what can be done, what is the third topic the Scrum Team addresses?

options.text: How the chosen work will get done, with the Developers planning the work needed to create the Increment
Who in management approves the selected items before work starts
When the team will hold the Sprint Review and Retrospective dates
How many story points the team completed in the previous Sprint

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The third Sprint Planning topic is how the chosen work will get done; for each selected item, the Developers plan the work necessary to create an Increment that meets the Definition of Done. Why the others are wrong: **B** Scrum requires no management approval of selected items; **C** scheduling event dates is logistics, not a Sprint Planning topic; **D** reviewing past points is not the defined third topic.

questions.stem: A stakeholder treats the Sprint Review as a formal phase-gate approval where she signs off before the team may proceed. How should the Sprint Review be understood instead?

options.text: As a one-way demo where the team presents and stakeholders silently observe
As a formal approval gate that the team must pass to continue
As the event where the team reflects privately on its own process
As a working session where the Scrum Team and stakeholders collaborate on what was done and what to do next

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** The Sprint Review is a working session, not a mere demo or sign-off; the Scrum Team and stakeholders collaborate on the Increment, progress toward the Product Goal, and what to do next. Why the others are wrong: **A** it is collaborative, not a silent one-way demo; **B** Scrum has no phase-gate sign-off, and the team is not blocked awaiting approval; **C** private process reflection is the Sprint Retrospective.

questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of the Sprint Retrospective?

options.text: To plan how the team will increase quality and effectiveness by inspecting people, interactions, processes, tools, and the Definition of Done
To demonstrate the Increment to stakeholders and gather product feedback
To select the Product Backlog items for the next Sprint
To let the Product Owner reorder the Product Backlog with the team

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The Sprint Retrospective's purpose is to plan ways to increase quality and effectiveness by inspecting how the last Sprint went regarding individuals, interactions, processes, tools, and the Definition of Done. Why the others are wrong: **B** demonstrating the Increment to stakeholders is the Sprint Review; **C** selecting items for the next Sprint is Sprint Planning; **D** ongoing backlog reordering is Product Owner work, not the Retrospective's purpose.

questions.stem: A Daily Scrum is scheduled at a different time and place each day to fit people's calendars, and Developers say it feels chaotic. What does the Scrum Guide recommend about its timing?

options.text: The Daily Scrum should rotate times daily to share the inconvenience fairly
The Daily Scrum is held at the same time and place every working day of the Sprint to reduce complexity
The Daily Scrum should be held only on days when blockers exist
The ScrumMaster chooses a new time each morning based on availability

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** To reduce complexity, the Daily Scrum is held at the same time and place every working day of the Sprint. Why the others are wrong: **A** rotating the time adds the very complexity Scrum tries to remove; **C** the Daily Scrum happens every working day, not only when blockers arise; **D** the ScrumMaster does not pick a new time daily, and the event belongs to the Developers.

questions.stem: Midway through a one-month Sprint, the Developers realize they selected far more work than they can complete. How does Scrum expect them to handle the Sprint Backlog?

options.text: They must deliver every selected item regardless, since the Sprint Backlog is fixed
They extend the Sprint by a week to fit all the items
They cancel the Sprint because the plan was wrong
They renegotiate the scope of selected work with the Product Owner as more is learned, keeping the Sprint Goal intact

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** The Sprint Backlog is updated throughout the Sprint as more is learned, and the scope may be clarified and renegotiated with the Product Owner as needed, while the Sprint Goal remains the fixed commitment. Why the others are wrong: **A** the Sprint Backlog is not a frozen contract of every item; **B** Sprints have a fixed length and are not extended; **C** falling behind is not grounds to cancel a Sprint.

questions.stem: Which two statements about the Daily Scrum are correct according to the Scrum Guide? (Select two.)

options.text: It is an event for the Developers of the Scrum Team
The Developers may adjust their plan for the upcoming day of work during it
It is the only time Developers may adjust their plan or talk during the Sprint
The ScrumMaster must run it and assign the next tasks

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** The Daily Scrum is an event for the Developers, who use it to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adjust their plan for the upcoming day of work. Why the others are wrong: **C** Developers can meet and adjust their plan throughout the day; the Daily Scrum is not the only allowed time; **D** if the ScrumMaster or Product Owner participates as a Developer they take part, but the ScrumMaster does not run it or assign tasks.

questions.stem: Within a single Sprint Planning session, order these three topics as the Scrum Guide presents them, from first to last.

options.text: Why is this Sprint valuable? (craft the Sprint Goal)
What can be Done this Sprint? (select Product Backlog items)
How will the chosen work get done? (plan the work)

questions.explanation: Sprint Planning addresses three topics in sequence. First the Scrum Team discusses why the Sprint is valuable and the Product Owner proposes how the product could increase value, leading the team to craft the Sprint Goal. Next the Developers, in conversation with the Product Owner, select which Product Backlog items to include, deciding what can be Done this Sprint. Finally, for each selected item the Developers plan how the work will get done to produce an Increment that meets the Definition of Done.

questions.stem: A finance department insists each Scrum Team submit a fixed annual scope and budget locked twelve months in advance. Why might the ScrumMaster work with the organization to change this?

options.text: Because locking scope and budget a year ahead conflicts with empirical, adaptive planning and the team's ability to inspect and adapt
Because Scrum forbids any form of budgeting whatsoever
Because the ScrumMaster should personally set every team's annual budget
Because finance, not the Product Owner, should own the Product Backlog

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A rigidly locked annual scope undermines empiricism, where plans adapt as the team learns; the ScrumMaster helps the organization shift toward funding and planning approaches that allow inspection and adaptation. Why the others are wrong: **B** Scrum does not forbid budgeting; it favors adaptive over fixed long-range commitments; **C** the ScrumMaster does not set budgets; **D** the Product Owner, not finance, owns the Product Backlog.

questions.stem: A team treats Product Backlog refinement as a mandatory weekly meeting with a fixed two-hour time-box. What does the Scrum Guide actually say about refinement?

options.text: Refinement is a formal Scrum event with its own fixed time-box
Refinement is an ongoing activity to add detail, estimates, and order to Product Backlog items
Refinement is performed solely by the Product Owner in isolation
Refinement is prohibited during a Sprint and only allowed between Sprints

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Product Backlog refinement is the ongoing act of breaking down and further defining Product Backlog items into smaller, more precise items, adding details such as a description, order, and size. Why the others are wrong: **A** refinement is an ongoing activity, not one of the five formal events with a time-box; **C** the Developers who will do the work are responsible for sizing, so it is collaborative, not the Product Owner alone; **D** refinement happens continuously, including during a Sprint.

questions.stem: A team wants to know what the commitments add to the three Scrum artifacts. Which statement best captures the purpose of the commitments?

options.text: They are optional labels that add no real value to the artifacts
They replace the need for the Scrum events
They reinforce empiricism and the Scrum values by giving each artifact a measure of progress and focus
They are management targets that the team must hit exactly

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Each artifact contains a commitment (Product Goal, Sprint Goal, Definition of Done) that exists to reinforce empiricism and the Scrum values, providing focus and a measure of progress against which to inspect. Why the others are wrong: **A** the commitments are integral, not optional labels; **B** commitments do not replace the events, which remain the formal inspect-and-adapt opportunities; **D** they are not rigid management quotas to hit exactly.

questions.stem: How does the Scrum Guide describe the Product Goal in relation to the Product Backlog?

options.text: It is a detailed release schedule listing every item's due date
It is a daily target the Developers set at each Daily Scrum
It is the same thing as the Sprint Goal
It is the long-term objective for the Scrum Team that the Product Backlog emerges to fulfill

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** The Product Goal is the long-term objective for the Scrum Team and the commitment of the Product Backlog; the backlog emerges to define what will fulfill that goal. Why the others are wrong: **A** it is an objective, not a dated release schedule; **B** it is a long-term product objective, not a daily target; **C** the Sprint Goal is a single-Sprint objective and the commitment of the Sprint Backlog, which is distinct from the Product Goal.

questions.stem: A leader proposes letting the team carry unfinished, undone work forward as part of the released Increment to hit a deadline. Why does this conflict with Scrum?

options.text: It does not conflict; partially finished work counts as an Increment
Work that does not meet the Definition of Done cannot be released or presented as part of the Increment
Only the ScrumMaster may declare unfinished work to be Done
The Definition of Done applies only to the final Sprint of a release

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The moment a Product Backlog item meets the Definition of Done, an Increment is born; work that does not meet the Definition of Done cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review. Why the others are wrong: **A** partially finished work is explicitly not an Increment; **C** no one can simply declare undone work Done; meeting the Definition of Done is the criterion; **D** the Definition of Done applies to every Increment, not just the last Sprint.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains how a clear Sprint Goal helps the Developers during the Sprint?

options.text: It forbids any change to the selected Product Backlog items
It guarantees the exact number of items the team will finish
It provides focus and coherence, encouraging the team to work together rather than on separate initiatives
It transfers ownership of the Sprint Backlog to the Product Owner

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** The Sprint Goal is the single objective for the Sprint; it creates focus and coherence, encouraging the Developers to work together rather than on separate initiatives. Why the others are wrong: **A** selected items can be renegotiated; the goal stays fixed but the scope can flex; **B** it does not guarantee a fixed item count; **D** the Developers own the Sprint Backlog, not the Product Owner.

questions.stem: Which two are genuine advantages of a strong, shared Definition of Done? (Select two.)

options.text: It creates transparency about what 'done' really means for everyone
It improves the quality and usability of each Increment
It lets the team skip testing because quality is assumed
It allows partially complete items to be reported as finished

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** A strong Definition of Done creates a shared, transparent understanding of completeness and raises the quality and usability of every Increment. Why the others are wrong: **C** a strong Definition of Done typically requires testing rather than allowing it to be skipped; **D** it prevents, not enables, presenting partially complete items as finished.

questions.stem: A Retrospective is dominated by two senior Developers while quieter members stay silent. Which facilitation technique best surfaces everyone's input?

options.text: Let the senior Developers continue since they have the most experience
Use a silent-writing or round-robin technique so every participant contributes before open discussion
Have the ScrumMaster decide the improvements and announce them
Cancel the Retrospective to avoid conflict

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Techniques such as silent writing or round-robin give every participant an equal chance to contribute before open discussion, reducing dominance by a few voices and improving the quality of group decision making. Why the others are wrong: **A** allowing a few to dominate suppresses valuable input and harms safety; **C** the ScrumMaster deciding for the team undermines self-management; **D** cancelling removes the team's key inspect-and-adapt opportunity.

questions.stem: A Developer asks the ScrumMaster directly, 'What does the Definition of Done mean and why do we keep one?' Which stance is the ScrumMaster primarily using if she explains the concept clearly?

options.text: Coaching
Mentoring
Teaching
Facilitating

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Explaining a specific concept such as the Definition of Done is teaching, the stance of imparting concrete knowledge or skills. Why the others are wrong: **A** coaching would use questions to help the Developer find their own understanding rather than supplying the explanation; **B** mentoring shares personal experience through an ongoing relationship, which is not what a direct concept explanation is; **D** facilitating helps a group converge on a decision, not impart a definition to one person.

questions.stem: The same impediment, a flaky shared test environment, keeps reappearing Sprint after Sprint. Which technique best addresses the root cause rather than the symptom?

options.text: Restart the test environment each morning and move on
Facilitate a root-cause analysis, such as the Five Whys, so the team tackles the underlying source
Stop tracking the impediment so it no longer appears on the board
Tell the Developers to ignore failures from that environment

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A recurring impediment signals an unaddressed root cause; facilitating a root-cause technique such as the Five Whys helps the team find and resolve the underlying source rather than repeatedly patching the symptom. Why the others are wrong: **A** restarting daily treats the symptom and lets the impediment recur; **C** hiding the impediment reduces transparency without solving anything; **D** ignoring failures masks real defects and erodes quality.

questions.stem: Which development practice most directly reduces technical debt by keeping the design clean as code evolves?

options.text: Continuous refactoring to improve internal structure without changing external behavior
Deferring all design improvements until a dedicated cleanup project years later
Copying and pasting code to avoid touching existing modules
Disabling failing tests so the build always passes

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Continuous refactoring improves the internal structure of the code without changing its external behavior, keeping the design clean and limiting the technical debt that otherwise accumulates. Why the others are wrong: **B** deferring design improvements lets debt compound over time; **C** copy-paste duplication increases debt and maintenance cost; **D** disabling failing tests hides defects and is itself a form of debt.

questions.stem: A ScrumMaster wants the team to converge quickly on a few options from a long brainstormed list during a workshop. Which facilitation technique fits best?

options.text: Dot voting, where participants place a limited number of votes on the options they favor
Having the loudest participant pick the options
Postponing any selection indefinitely
Letting the ScrumMaster unilaterally choose the options

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Dot voting is a simple group decision-making technique that quickly narrows a large set of options by letting each participant allocate a limited number of votes, surfacing the group's collective preference. Why the others are wrong: **B** deferring to the loudest voice ignores the group and harms participation; **C** postponing the selection resolves nothing; **D** the ScrumMaster choosing alone undermines the team's self-management.

questions.stem: Which two behaviors best reflect a coaching stance rather than a directive one? (Select two.)

options.text: Asking open, powerful questions that help the team explore options
Holding space and listening so the team reaches its own insight
Prescribing the exact solution and timeline for the team to follow
Approving each technical decision before the team may act

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Coaching is non-directive: it relies on open, powerful questions and active listening so people reach their own insights and build lasting capability. Why the others are wrong: **C** prescribing the solution and timeline is directive consulting or telling, not coaching; **D** approving every decision is command-and-control that removes the team's autonomy.

questions.stem: Which action is a way the ScrumMaster serves the Product Owner specifically?

options.text: Helping establish empirical product planning for a complex environment
Assigning daily tasks to the Developers on the Product Owner's behalf
Approving the Increment for release each Sprint
Writing the team's performance evaluations

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The Scrum Guide lists helping establish empirical product planning for a complex environment among the ways the ScrumMaster serves the Product Owner. Why the others are wrong: **B** assigning Developer tasks contradicts self-management and is not a service to the Product Owner; **C** the Product Owner, not the ScrumMaster, decides on releasing the Increment; **D** writing performance evaluations is not a ScrumMaster service.

questions.stem: An organization keeps a separate, full-time 'resource manager' to load-balance individuals across several Scrum Teams. Why might the ScrumMaster treat this as an organizational impediment?

options.text: Because it perfectly supports stable, cross-functional, self-managing teams
Because Scrum requires every organization to employ a resource manager
Because shuffling individuals undermines stable, cross-functional, self-managing teams and the cohesion Scrum relies on
Because resource managers must always approve the Sprint Backlog

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Continuously shuffling individuals between teams undermines the stability, cross-functionality, and cohesion that self-managing Scrum Teams depend on, so the ScrumMaster helps the organization recognize and reduce this impediment. Why the others are wrong: **A** the practice harms rather than supports stable teams; **B** Scrum does not require a resource manager; **D** no one outside the Developers approves the Sprint Backlog.

questions.stem: Leadership asks the ScrumMaster to produce a traditional Gantt chart and act as the single point of status for a 'project.' Considering that Scrum has no project manager, what is the best response?

options.text: Accept the project manager duties since the ScrumMaster is the closest equivalent
Coach leadership on Scrum's empirical transparency, where the Product Owner communicates progress toward the Product Goal and the team's artifacts make status visible
Tell leadership that progress cannot be communicated in Scrum
Hand the request to the Developers to manage as a side project

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Scrum has no project manager; transparency comes from the artifacts and from the Product Owner communicating progress toward the Product Goal, so the ScrumMaster coaches leadership toward these empirical mechanisms instead of recreating the role. Why the others are wrong: **A** assuming project-manager duties contradicts Scrum's distributed accountabilities; **C** progress is communicated, just empirically rather than via a fixed plan; **D** dumping it on the Developers as a side project is not how Scrum provides transparency.

questions.stem: Several Scrum Teams build one product but each keeps its own conflicting Product Backlog. How can the ScrumMaster support an effective product backlog management approach across them?

options.text: Encourage even more separate backlogs so each team is fully independent
Help the organization recognize that multiple teams on one product should share a single Product Backlog and Product Goal with one Product Owner
Have each ScrumMaster own a slice of the backlog
Let the Developers vote weekly on which backlog wins

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The Scrum Guide notes that if multiple Scrum Teams work on one product, they share one Product Backlog, one Product Goal, and one Product Owner; the ScrumMaster helps the organization move toward this to keep backlog management effective. Why the others are wrong: **A** more separate backlogs deepen the conflict; **C** ScrumMasters do not own portions of the backlog; **D** voting between rival backlogs does not establish a single coherent backlog.

questions.stem: Which two are ways the ScrumMaster serves the wider organization, as described by the Scrum Guide? (Select two.)

options.text: Planning and advising Scrum implementations within the organization
Removing barriers between stakeholders and Scrum Teams
Personally signing off every Increment before release
Setting compensation levels for the Developers

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** The ScrumMaster serves the organization by planning and advising Scrum implementations and by removing barriers between stakeholders and Scrum Teams. Why the others are wrong: **C** the Product Owner, not the ScrumMaster, decides on releasing the Increment, and Scrum has no sign-off gate; **D** setting compensation is a management function outside the ScrumMaster's defined service.

questions.stem: A Developer shares an unfinished prototype and openly says she is unsure it will work, inviting feedback early. Which Scrum value is she most directly demonstrating?

options.text: Focus
Openness
Commitment
Respect

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Openness is the Scrum value of being open about the work and the challenges, which is exactly what sharing an uncertain prototype for early feedback demonstrates. Why the others are wrong: **A** focus concerns concentrating on the Sprint's work, not transparency about doubts; **C** commitment is dedication to goals, not candor about uncertainty; **D** respect is valuing others as capable people, which is not the central act here.

questions.stem: A senior engineer assumes a junior teammate cannot handle a complex task and quietly redoes the work without telling her. Which Scrum value is most clearly being violated?

options.text: Respect
Focus
Commitment
Courage

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Respect means treating teammates as capable, independent people; assuming a colleague cannot handle work and silently redoing it disrespects her competence. Why the others are wrong: **B** focus is about concentrating on the Sprint's work, not how teammates regard each other; **C** commitment concerns dedication to goals; **D** courage is about doing the right thing under pressure, not the issue of valuing others here.

questions.stem: The Scrum Guide states that the Scrum values build something essential among team members that makes empiricism and self-management actually work. What is it?

options.text: A detailed audit trail of every decision
Trust
A fixed long-term plan
Individual performance rankings

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The Scrum Guide says that when the five values are embodied by the Scrum Team, the pillars of transparency, inspection, and adaptation come to life and build trust. Why the others are wrong: **A** an audit trail is documentation, not what the values create; **C** a fixed long-term plan contradicts the adaptive, empirical mindset the values support; **D** individual rankings work against the whole-team trust the values are meant to foster.

questions.stem: Which statement best reflects the Agile Manifesto principle about how to build projects and trust the people involved?

options.text: Build projects around motivated individuals, giving them the environment and support they need, and trust them to get the job done
Build projects around detailed processes and require sign-off at every step
Assign work top-down and supervise individuals closely to ensure compliance
Replace people frequently to keep costs as low as possible

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** An Agile Manifesto principle says to build projects around motivated individuals, give them the environment and support they need, and trust them to get the job done. Why the others are wrong: **B** relying on heavy process and sign-offs is the document-driven approach the Manifesto moves away from; **C** close top-down supervision contradicts trusting motivated people; **D** churning people through a project undermines the support and trust the principle calls for.
