questions.stem: A team works long overtime hours every Sprint to keep up, and burnout is rising. Which Agile Manifesto principle most directly speaks to this situation?

options.text: Working software is the primary measure of progress
Agile processes promote sustainable development; sponsors, developers, and users should be able to maintain a constant pace indefinitely
Simplicity, the art of maximizing the amount of work not done, is essential
The best architectures emerge from self-organizing teams

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** This principle states that agile processes promote sustainable development and that everyone involved should be able to maintain a constant pace indefinitely, directly addressing chronic overtime and burnout. Why the others are wrong: **A** measuring progress by working software does not address pace; **C** simplicity is about minimizing unnecessary work, not work hours; **D** self-organizing architecture is unrelated to sustainable pace.

questions.stem: According to the Scrum Guide, which two statements correctly describe how inspection and adaptation relate to transparency? (Select two.)

options.text: Inspection enables adaptation; inspection without adaptation is considered pointless
If artifacts have low transparency, inspection can be misleading and adaptation may make things worse
Adaptation should be delayed until transparency reaches one hundred percent certainty
Transparency is optional as long as the team inspects frequently

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** The Scrum Guide states inspection enables adaptation and that inspection without adaptation is pointless, and it warns that low transparency can lead to decisions that diminish value and increase risk. Why the others are wrong: **C** Scrum never requires perfect certainty before adapting; empiricism adapts on evidence as it emerges; **D** transparency is essential, not optional, because it is what makes inspection meaningful.

questions.stem: A Product Owner asks what their single overarching accountability is, beyond the day-to-day backlog tasks. Which answer best matches the Scrum Guide?

options.text: Guaranteeing the team delivers a fixed number of items per Sprint
Managing the Developers' day-to-day tasks
Maximizing the value of the product resulting from the work of the Scrum Team
Removing all impediments the team encounters

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** The Scrum Guide states the Product Owner is accountable for maximizing the value of the product resulting from the work of the Scrum Team. Why the others are wrong: **A** Scrum makes no per-Sprint item-count guarantee, and value is the focus, not raw output; **B** the self-managing Developers decide their own work; the Product Owner does not manage their tasks; **D** causing the removal of impediments is the Scrum Master's accountability.

questions.stem: In which way does the Scrum Master serve the Scrum Team according to the Scrum Guide?

options.text: By assigning each Developer their daily tasks
By helping the Scrum Team focus on creating high-value Increments that meet the Definition of Done
By approving the Product Backlog order each Sprint
By writing the team's user stories

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Among the Scrum Master's services to the Scrum Team, the Scrum Guide lists helping the team focus on creating high-value Increments that meet the Definition of Done. Why the others are wrong: **A** assigning daily tasks contradicts the Developers' self-management; **C** ordering the Product Backlog is the Product Owner's accountability; **D** authoring stories is work for the Product Owner and Developers, not a Scrum Master service.

questions.stem: A stakeholder wants to influence what the product becomes but is frustrated that they cannot directly edit the Product Backlog. How does the Scrum Guide describe the Product Owner's interface with stakeholders?

options.text: Stakeholders may edit the Product Backlog directly whenever the Product Owner is unavailable
The Product Owner represents the needs of many stakeholders in the Product Backlog, and stakeholders influence the product by working with the Product Owner
Stakeholders must route all input through the Scrum Master, who edits the backlog
The Developers collect stakeholder requests and order the backlog themselves

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The Product Owner may represent the needs of many stakeholders in the Product Backlog, and those wanting to change it can do so by trying to convince the Product Owner. Why the others are wrong: **A** stakeholders never edit the backlog directly; the Product Owner is accountable for it; **C** the Scrum Master does not edit the backlog on stakeholders' behalf; **D** ordering the Product Backlog is the Product Owner's accountability, not the Developers'.

questions.stem: A Scrum Master is told their job is mainly to schedule and run all four Scrum events as a coordinator. Which framing better captures the Scrum Master's accountability per the Scrum Guide?

options.text: The Scrum Master is accountable for the Scrum Team's effectiveness and for establishing Scrum as defined in the Scrum Guide, helping everyone enact it
The Scrum Master is accountable for the team hitting its committed scope every Sprint
The Scrum Master is accountable for writing the Sprint Backlog for the Developers
The Scrum Master is accountable for approving the Increment before the Sprint Review

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The Scrum Guide says the Scrum Master is accountable for the Scrum Team's effectiveness and for establishing Scrum as defined in the Guide, helping the team and organization understand and enact it. Why the others are wrong: **B** Scrum does not treat scope as a fixed per-Sprint commitment the Scrum Master must guarantee; **C** the Developers own the Sprint Backlog; **D** no one approves the Increment as a gate, and that is not a Scrum Master accountability.

questions.stem: The Developers debate who decides the technical approach for turning selected Product Backlog items into an Increment. What does the Scrum Guide say?

options.text: The Product Owner dictates the technical approach to ensure value
The Scrum Master selects the architecture for the Developers
The Developers are always accountable for deciding how to turn Product Backlog items into Increments of value
An external architect must approve the approach before work begins

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** The Scrum Guide states the Developers are always accountable for things including instilling quality and deciding how the work is done; they create the plan and the technical approach for the Increment. Why the others are wrong: **A** the Product Owner is accountable for value, not for dictating technical design; **B** the Scrum Master coaches but does not choose the architecture; **D** Scrum defines no external approval gate for the Developers' technical decisions.

questions.stem: According to the Scrum Guide, which two are characteristics of the Scrum Team as a whole? (Select two.)

options.text: It is cross-functional, with members who together have all the skills needed to create value each Sprint
It is self-managing, deciding internally who does what, when, and how
It is divided into permanent specialist sub-teams with their own leads
It reports to a separate delivery manager who controls the work

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** The Scrum Guide describes the Scrum Team as cross-functional, with the skills needed to create value each Sprint, and as self-managing, internally deciding who does what, when, and how. Why the others are wrong: **C** the Scrum Team has no sub-teams or hierarchies; it is one cohesive unit; **D** there is no separate delivery manager controlling the team in Scrum.

questions.stem: An organization runs one product with several Scrum Teams and asks how many Product Owners and Product Goals there should be. What does the Scrum Guide indicate?

options.text: Each team should have its own Product Owner and its own Product Goal
There should be one Product Owner and one Product Goal for the product, even with multiple teams
Product Owners are optional once more than one team is involved
The number of Product Owners should equal the number of stakeholders

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A Scrum Team focuses on one Product Goal at a time, and when multiple Scrum Teams work on one product they share one Product Backlog, one Product Goal, and one Product Owner. Why the others are wrong: **A** separate goals per team fragments a single product's direction; **C** every product needs a Product Owner accountable for value; **D** the count of Product Owners is not tied to the number of stakeholders.

questions.stem: What is the maximum time-box for the Sprint Review for a one-month Sprint?

options.text: One hour
Two hours
Eight hours
Four hours

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** The Sprint Review is time-boxed to a maximum of four hours for a one-month Sprint and is usually shorter for shorter Sprints. Why the others are wrong: **A** one hour is well below the maximum for a one-month Sprint; **B** two hours is also below the four-hour limit; **C** eight hours is the maximum for Sprint Planning, not the Sprint Review.

questions.stem: What is the maximum time-box for the Sprint Retrospective for a one-month Sprint?

options.text: Fifteen minutes
Eight hours
There is no time-box for the Retrospective
Three hours

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** The Sprint Retrospective is time-boxed to a maximum of three hours for a one-month Sprint and is usually shorter for shorter Sprints. Why the others are wrong: **A** fifteen minutes is the Daily Scrum's time-box, not the Retrospective's; **B** eight hours is the maximum for Sprint Planning; **C** the Retrospective does have a time-box in the Scrum Guide.

questions.stem: Who, beyond the Scrum Team, does the Scrum Guide say attends the Sprint Review, and why?

options.text: No one outside the Scrum Team may attend the Sprint Review
The Scrum Team invites key stakeholders to collaborate on the Increment and progress toward the Product Goal
Only executives attend, to formally approve the Sprint
Customers attend solely to sign a contract acceptance form

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The Scrum Guide says the Scrum Team presents the results of their work to key stakeholders and that the Sprint Review is a working session where they collaborate on what was accomplished and what to do next. Why the others are wrong: **A** stakeholders are explicitly invited, so the event is not closed; **C** it is a collaborative working session, not an executive approval gate; **D** the purpose is collaboration on the product, not contract sign-off.

questions.stem: Developers insist the Daily Scrum must always follow the three classic questions (what I did, what I will do, blockers). What does the 2020 Scrum Guide actually say about the Daily Scrum's structure?

options.text: The three-questions format is mandatory in the 2020 Scrum Guide
The Developers may select whatever structure and techniques they want, as long as the Daily Scrum focuses on progress toward the Sprint Goal
The Scrum Master must dictate the Daily Scrum format
The Daily Scrum has no purpose, so any conversation is equally valid

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The 2020 Scrum Guide removed any required format; the Developers can select whatever structure and techniques they want, provided the Daily Scrum focuses on progress toward the Sprint Goal and produces an actionable plan. Why the others are wrong: **A** the three questions are no longer prescribed; **C** the Daily Scrum belongs to the Developers, not the Scrum Master; **D** the event has a clear purpose, so it is not just any conversation.

questions.stem: An executive complains that fixed-length Sprints feel rigid. Which benefit of the Sprint's fixed cadence does the Scrum Guide emphasize?

options.text: Fixed-length Sprints enable predictability by ensuring inspection and adaptation toward the Product Goal at least every calendar month
Fixed-length Sprints guarantee the same number of features every time
Fixed-length Sprints remove the need to inspect progress
Fixed-length Sprints exist mainly to give managers strict deadlines

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The Scrum Guide says Sprints enable predictability by ensuring inspection and adaptation of progress toward the Product Goal at least every calendar month. Why the others are wrong: **B** Scrum makes no guarantee of equal feature counts; predictability is about regular inspection, not fixed output; **C** Sprints exist precisely to create regular inspection, not remove it; **D** the cadence serves the team's empiricism, not management deadlines.

questions.stem: A manager pressures the Developers to lower quality this Sprint to fit more features in, promising to fix it later. What does the Scrum Guide say about quality and the Sprint?

options.text: Quality may be reduced temporarily as long as it is restored within two Sprints
Quality goals do not decrease during the Sprint; the Developers maintain quality by adhering to the Definition of Done while scope may be clarified and renegotiated
Only the Sprint Goal matters, so quality is irrelevant within a Sprint
The Scrum Master may authorize lowering quality to meet a deadline

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The Scrum Guide states that during the Sprint quality does not decrease, and that scope may be clarified and renegotiated with the Product Owner as more is learned, while the Definition of Done is upheld. Why the others are wrong: **A** Scrum has no concept of temporarily reducing quality; **C** quality is integral, not irrelevant, to a usable Increment; **D** no one is authorized to lower quality to hit a deadline.

questions.stem: According to the Scrum Guide, which two benefits does the Daily Scrum provide besides inspecting progress toward the Sprint Goal? (Select two.)

options.text: It replaces the Sprint Review for stakeholders
It is where the Product Owner reorders the Product Backlog daily
It improves communications and identifies impediments
It promotes quick decision making and reduces the need for other meetings

questions.explanation: **Correct (C, D):** The Scrum Guide notes that Daily Scrums improve communications, identify impediments, promote quick decision making, and consequently eliminate the need for other meetings. Why the others are wrong: **A** stakeholder collaboration on the product happens at the Sprint Review, not the Daily Scrum; **B** the Product Owner does not run a daily backlog reordering at the Daily Scrum.

questions.stem: Which two statements about the Sprint Review are correct according to the Scrum Guide? (Select two.)

options.text: It is the second-to-last event of the Sprint
The Product Backlog may be adjusted to meet new opportunities discussed during the review
It is intended to be a presentation limited to a one-way demo
It is where the Developers privately plan their personal improvements

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** The Sprint Review is the second-to-last event of the Sprint (before the Retrospective), and the Product Backlog may be adjusted to meet new opportunities that surface during the collaboration. Why the others are wrong: **C** the Scrum Guide cautions it is a working session and should not be limited to a presentation; **D** private process improvement belongs to the Sprint Retrospective, not the Review.

questions.stem: For a one-month Sprint, order these Scrum events from the shortest maximum time-box to the longest.

options.text: Daily Scrum (15 minutes)
Sprint Retrospective (up to 3 hours)
Sprint Review (up to 4 hours)
Sprint Planning (up to 8 hours)

questions.explanation: Ranking the events by their maximum time-box for a one-month Sprint gives a clear order. The Daily Scrum is the shortest at a fixed 15 minutes. The Sprint Retrospective is capped at three hours. The Sprint Review is capped at four hours. Sprint Planning is the longest, time-boxed to a maximum of eight hours. Each of these maximums is reduced proportionally for shorter Sprints, but the relative ordering stays the same.

questions.stem: The Scrum Guide says each artifact contains a commitment for a specific reason. What is the stated purpose of these commitments in relation to transparency?

options.text: They exist to enhance transparency and focus against which progress can be measured
They exist to give management strict quotas to enforce
They exist to replace the artifacts themselves
They exist purely as documentation with no effect on progress

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The Scrum Guide states that each artifact contains a commitment that exists to enhance transparency and focus against which progress can be measured. Why the others are wrong: **B** the commitments are not management quotas; they serve empiricism; **C** commitments accompany the artifacts; they do not replace them; **D** they actively provide a measure of progress, so they are not inert documentation.

questions.stem: How often, according to the Scrum Guide, should the Sprint Backlog be updated so it reflects the Developers' current plan?

options.text: Only at Sprint Planning, then frozen for the rest of the Sprint
It is updated throughout the Sprint as more is learned and is a highly visible, real-time picture of the work
Only at the Sprint Review, by the stakeholders
Once a week, by the Scrum Master

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The Scrum Guide describes the Sprint Backlog as a highly visible, real-time picture of the work the Developers plan to accomplish, updated throughout the Sprint as more is learned. Why the others are wrong: **A** it is not frozen after Sprint Planning; it emerges during the Sprint; **C** stakeholders do not update the Sprint Backlog at the Sprint Review; **D** it is not a weekly Scrum Master task but an ongoing Developer activity.

questions.stem: A new Scrum Team has no organizational Definition of Done to inherit. According to the Scrum Guide, what should they do?

options.text: Operate without any Definition of Done until management provides one
If there are no organizational standards, the Scrum Team must create a Definition of Done appropriate for the product
Ask the Scrum Master to write it alone and keep it secret
Borrow an unrelated team's Definition of Done verbatim and never change it

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The Scrum Guide says that if there are no organizational standards, the Scrum Team must create a Definition of Done appropriate for the product. Why the others are wrong: **A** a team should not produce Increments without a Definition of Done; **C** the whole Scrum Team shapes the Definition of Done, and it must be transparent, not secret; **D** copying an unrelated team's standard verbatim and freezing it ignores the product's real quality needs.

questions.stem: A team's Definition of Done is so weak that 'done' work still needs significant rework before release, and unaddressed debt keeps growing. How does the Scrum Guide connect the Definition of Done to managing this debt?

options.text: A weak Definition of Done has no relationship to technical debt

If the Definition of Done is not part of the team's standards, the Developers must still do work to meet release quality, and a stronger Definition of Done makes the true state of the Increment transparent so debt is not hidden
The Definition of Done should be removed to speed up delivery
Only the Product Owner is responsible for technical debt, not the Definition of Done

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A robust Definition of Done forces the work needed to reach release quality and keeps the true state of the Increment transparent, so accumulated technical debt is surfaced rather than hidden behind a false 'done.' Why the others are wrong: **A** a weak Definition of Done directly enables hidden debt; **C** removing it destroys transparency about quality; **D** the Developers, through the Definition of Done, instill quality; it is not solely the Product Owner's concern.

questions.stem: Leadership wants a single tool that Scrum mandates for tracking progress toward the Sprint Goal and Product Goal. What does the Scrum Guide say about such tracking practices?

options.text: Scrum mandates a burndown chart for every team
Scrum does not prescribe a specific practice; various trend-based practices may be used, but they do not replace the importance of empiricism
Scrum requires a burnup chart and a cumulative flow diagram together
Scrum forbids any progress tracking outside the events

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The Scrum Guide notes that various practices exist to forecast progress, such as burndowns, burnups, and cumulative flows, but while useful, these do not replace the importance of empiricism. Why the others are wrong: **A** no specific chart is mandated; **C** Scrum does not require any particular combination of charts; **D** Scrum does not forbid tracking; it simply does not prescribe one method.

questions.stem: Which two are valid ways a Scrum Team can create or strengthen its Definition of Done? (Select two.)

options.text: Adopt the organization's mandatory quality standards as a minimum baseline
Collaborate as a whole Scrum Team to agree on the quality criteria an Increment must meet to be releasable
Let each Developer keep a private, personal definition that others cannot see
Define 'done' as simply 'the code compiles,' ignoring testing and integration

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Where organizational standards exist they form a minimum the team must meet, and the whole Scrum Team collaborates to agree the quality criteria that make an Increment releasable. Why the others are wrong: **C** the Definition of Done must be shared and transparent, not private per person; **D** reducing 'done' to mere compilation ignores the quality measures required for the product and hides incomplete work.

questions.stem: Two departments outside the Scrum Team repeatedly clash over a shared dependency, slowing every Scrum Team that touches it. How can facilitation serve the wider organization here?

options.text: The Scrum Master facilitates a structured cross-department conversation so the groups surface interests and reach a workable agreement
The Scrum Master decides the outcome for both departments to save time
The Scrum Master refuses to get involved because facilitation only applies inside the team
The Scrum Master tells both departments to stop talking until they agree on their own

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Facilitation can serve the organization, not just the team; the Scrum Master stays neutral on content and helps the groups surface interests and converge on a workable agreement. Why the others are wrong: **B** imposing the outcome is the opposite of facilitation; **C** facilitation is explicitly useful beyond the team, including organizational impediments; **D** withholding any help and demanding silence does not facilitate a resolution.

questions.stem: A brand-new team has never used Scrum and asks the Scrum Master to explain how the events, artifacts, and accountabilities fit together. Which stance is the Scrum Master primarily using?

options.text: Teaching
Coaching
Mentoring
Facilitating

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Explaining how Scrum's parts fit together to people who do not yet know them is teaching, the stance of imparting specific knowledge or skills. Why the others are wrong: **B** coaching would use questions to help the team find their own understanding, not deliver the explanation; **C** mentoring shares the mentor's personal experience through an ongoing relationship; **D** facilitating helps a group reach a decision, which is not what explaining the framework is.

questions.stem: A newly promoted Scrum Master regularly meets a veteran Scrum Master who shares hard-won lessons and guides their professional growth over months. Which stance does the veteran primarily embody?

options.text: Facilitating
Mentoring
Teaching
Directing

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Mentoring shares the mentor's experience and guidance through an ongoing relationship over time, which is exactly what the veteran is doing for the new Scrum Master. Why the others are wrong: **A** facilitating is helping a group hold a productive conversation and decide, not one-on-one growth guidance; **C** teaching imparts specific knowledge or skills rather than longer-term experiential guidance; **D** directing means telling someone what to do, which mentoring is not.

questions.stem: Which behavior best exemplifies the servant-leadership stance the Scrum Guide associates with the Scrum Master?

options.text: Focusing on the needs of the team and the people they serve to help them grow and perform their best
Prioritizing the Scrum Master's own visibility to leadership above the team's needs
Withholding information so the team depends on the Scrum Master
Making all decisions centrally to keep tight control

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Servant leadership focuses on the needs of the team and the people they serve, helping them grow and perform as effectively as possible, which is the leadership the Scrum Master models. Why the others are wrong: **B** putting self-promotion above the team contradicts serving them; **C** creating dependence by hoarding information is the opposite of growing the team; **D** centralizing all decisions removes the self-management servant leaders cultivate.

questions.stem: An impediment clearly sits outside the Scrum Team's authority to resolve, such as a company-wide security policy blocking deployments. What is the most appropriate Scrum Master technique?

options.text: Ignore it because it is not the team's fault
Make the impediment transparent and escalate it to those in the organization who have the authority to address it
Instruct the Developers to bypass the security policy
Cancel the Sprint until the policy changes

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** When an impediment is beyond the team's control, the Scrum Master makes it transparent and works with or escalates to those in the organization empowered to remove it. Why the others are wrong: **A** ignoring it leaves the team blocked and abandons the Scrum Master's accountability to cause impediment removal; **C** bypassing a security policy is reckless and not impediment resolution; **D** only the Product Owner can cancel a Sprint, and a policy blocker is not grounds for it.

questions.stem: Which two development practices most directly help reduce technical debt and keep the Increment releasable? (Select two.)

options.text: Test-driven development, writing automated tests that drive and verify the code
Pair programming, with two Developers continuously reviewing the work as it is written
Accumulating untested code to be validated in a big-bang phase next quarter
Turning off automated checks whenever they slow the build

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Test-driven development builds in fast, automated verification, and pair programming provides continuous in-line review; both catch defects early and keep the design clean, limiting technical debt. Why the others are wrong: **C** deferring testing to a big-bang phase lets defects and debt pile up; **D** disabling automated checks removes a key quality feedback loop and increases debt.

questions.stem: A Product Owner is overwhelmed coordinating many stakeholders with conflicting demands. Which Scrum Master service is most directly relevant?

options.text: Taking over the Product Owner's decisions about backlog order
Telling stakeholders the Product Owner is unavailable indefinitely
Assigning the Developers to handle all stakeholder requests directly
Helping the Product Owner facilitate stakeholder collaboration as requested or needed

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** The Scrum Guide lists helping facilitate stakeholder collaboration as requested or needed among the ways the Scrum Master serves the Product Owner. Why the others are wrong: **A** taking over backlog ordering usurps the Product Owner's accountability; **B** cutting off stakeholders does not help the Product Owner manage value; **C** routing all stakeholder work to the Developers bypasses the Product Owner's accountability for the product.

questions.stem: An organization splits work across separate component teams, so building one feature requires handoffs among several teams and long waits. Why might the Scrum Master treat this as an organizational impediment?

options.text: Because component teams and handoffs work against cross-functional, value-delivering Scrum Teams and create delay and reduced ownership
Because Scrum requires every organization to use component teams
Because handoffs always speed up delivery
Because only the Product Owner is allowed to notice organizational structure

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Component teams and the handoffs between them undermine the cross-functional, value-focused team Scrum relies on, creating queues, delay, and diffused ownership, so the Scrum Master helps the organization recognize and reduce this impediment. Why the others are wrong: **B** Scrum favors cross-functional teams, not component teams; **C** handoffs add delay rather than speed; **D** identifying organizational impediments is part of the Scrum Master's service, not the Product Owner's exclusive concern.

questions.stem: A stakeholder group rarely engages with the Scrum Team, so feedback arrives too late to act on. Which Scrum Master service to the organization best addresses this?

options.text: Removing barriers between stakeholders and Scrum Teams so feedback flows in time to inspect and adapt
Banning stakeholders from the Sprint Review to reduce noise
Having the Developers stop seeking feedback altogether
Locking the Product Backlog so stakeholder input cannot change it

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The Scrum Guide lists removing barriers between stakeholders and Scrum Teams among the Scrum Master's services to the organization, which here restores timely feedback for inspection and adaptation. Why the others are wrong: **B** barring stakeholders from the Sprint Review removes a key collaboration point; **C** stopping feedback-seeking worsens the disconnect; **D** locking the backlog blocks the adaptation that stakeholder input should inform.

questions.stem: A manager argues that because Scrum has no project manager, no one is accountable for managing the people and the budget, so chaos is inevitable. What is the most accurate reframing?

options.text: Scrum's lack of a project manager means accountability is simply abandoned

Scrum distributes the work traditionally bundled into a project manager across the three accountabilities, and people-management concerns like budgets remain organizational functions outside the Scrum Team's defined accountabilities
The Scrum Master silently absorbs every former project-manager duty, including budgets and HR
Scrum requires re-adding a project manager whenever budgets are involved

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Scrum defines no project manager and spreads that work across the Product Owner, Developers, and Scrum Master; line-management matters such as budgets and personnel are organizational functions, not Scrum Team accountabilities, so nothing is left ungoverned. Why the others are wrong: **A** accountability is redistributed, not abandoned; **C** the Scrum Master is a servant leader, not a catch-all for budgets and HR; **D** Scrum does not reintroduce a project manager for budgeting.

questions.stem: A Product Owner working in a fast-changing market wants help planning the product without locking a rigid multi-year roadmap. Which Scrum Master service fits best?

options.text: Helping establish empirical product planning for a complex environment
Producing a fixed three-year feature roadmap the team must follow exactly
Telling the Product Owner that planning is forbidden in Scrum
Handing product planning to the Developers as a permanent duty

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The Scrum Guide lists helping establish empirical product planning for a complex environment among the Scrum Master's services to the Product Owner, fitting a market where the plan must adapt to what is learned. Why the others are wrong: **B** a rigid multi-year roadmap contradicts empirical, adaptive planning; **C** Scrum supports planning, just empirically rather than fixed long-range; **D** product planning is the Product Owner's accountability, not a permanent Developer duty.

questions.stem: Senior leaders treat Scrum as a way to make the team produce more output faster, with no change to how the organization plans complex work. How should the Scrum Master serve the organization here?

options.text: Help employees and stakeholders understand and enact an empirical approach for complex work, reframing Scrum as a way to manage uncertainty rather than just increase output
Agree that Scrum is purely an output-acceleration tool
Promise leadership a fixed increase in features per Sprint
Avoid engaging leadership because culture is not the Scrum Master's concern

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A core service to the organization is helping employees and stakeholders understand and enact an empirical approach to complex work, so the Scrum Master reframes Scrum as managing uncertainty through inspection and adaptation, not merely producing more. Why the others are wrong: **B** treating Scrum as pure output acceleration misrepresents empiricism; **C** Scrum makes no fixed output guarantees; **D** coaching the organization on empiricism is squarely part of the Scrum Master's service.

flashcards.front: What are the three pillars of empiricism in Scrum?
flashcards.back: Transparency, inspection, and adaptation. Decisions are based on what is observed; the artifacts and progress must be transparent so that inspection leads to useful adaptation.

flashcards.front: What are the five Scrum values?
flashcards.back: Commitment, focus, openness, respect, and courage. Living these values builds the trust that makes empiricism and self-management work.

flashcards.front: Is Scrum a methodology or a framework?
flashcards.back: A lightweight framework. It is purposefully incomplete, defining only the parts needed to implement Scrum theory; teams add complementary practices that fit their context.

flashcards.front: What are the three accountabilities on a Scrum Team?
flashcards.back: The Scrum Master, the Product Owner, and the Developers. The 2020 Scrum Guide calls them accountabilities, not roles, and there is one Scrum Team, not separate sub-teams.

flashcards.front: Why is the Product Owner one person, not a committee?
flashcards.back: So the Product Backlog has a single, clear voice and accountability. A committee can represent its needs through the one Product Owner; to change the backlog, people must convince that person.

flashcards.front: Which event is the container for all other Scrum events?
flashcards.back: The Sprint. It is a fixed-length event of one month or less that holds Sprint Planning, the Daily Scrums, the Sprint Review, and the Sprint Retrospective. A new Sprint starts immediately after the previous one ends.

flashcards.front: What are the time-boxes for the Daily Scrum and Sprint Planning (one-month Sprint)?
flashcards.back: The Daily Scrum is 15 minutes. Sprint Planning is time-boxed to a maximum of 8 hours for a one-month Sprint and is usually shorter for shorter Sprints.

flashcards.front: Who can cancel a Sprint, and when?
flashcards.back: Only the Product Owner can cancel a Sprint, and it may be cancelled if the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete. Cancelling a Sprint is uncommon.

flashcards.front: What are the three Scrum artifacts and their commitments?
flashcards.back: Product Backlog — commitment is the Product Goal; Sprint Backlog — commitment is the Sprint Goal; Increment — commitment is the Definition of Done.

flashcards.front: What is the Definition of Done?
flashcards.back: A formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product. Work is not part of an Increment until it meets the Definition of Done.

flashcards.front: How do facilitating, teaching, mentoring, and coaching differ?
flashcards.back: Facilitating helps a group hold a productive conversation and decide (facilitator stays content-neutral). Teaching transfers specific knowledge or skills. Mentoring shares experience through an ongoing relationship. Coaching uses questions to help people find their own answers.

flashcards.front: Does Scrum have a project manager?
flashcards.back: No. Scrum defines no project manager; the work is distributed across the three accountabilities — the Product Owner owns value and the backlog, the Developers self-manage the work, and the Scrum Master enables the team's and organization's effectiveness.
